title: k-means clustering
summary: k-means finds k groups in unlabelled data by alternating two steps: assign every point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points. Each step can only lower the inertia (total squared distance to the assigned centres), so it converges, but possibly to a poor local minimum, which smarter starts (k-means++) and several runs guard against. Choose k with an elbow plot, and remember k-means assumes round, similarly sized clusters.
llm_link: Vector databases used for retrieval often run k-means over millions of embeddings: a query is compared only with the points in the few nearest clusters (an inverted-file index), and product quantisation compresses vectors by storing indices of nearby k-means centres.
key_ideas: Clustering is unsupervised: there are no labels, only data, and the method looks for natural groups.
k-means: assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points, repeat until nothing changes.
Inertia J = Σ‖xᵢ − μ_c(i)‖² never increases at either step, and it cannot go below 0, so the algorithm stops.
It can stop in a local minimum. k-means++ spreads the initial centres; run several times and keep the lowest inertia.
Choose k at the elbow of inertia versus k. Boundaries are straight lines between centres, so curved or nested clusters defeat it.

quiz.q: In the update step, where does each centre move?
options: To the point farthest from it
To the mean of the points currently assigned to it
quiz.explain: The mean is the single location that minimises the total squared distance to a group of points, so this step can only lower the inertia.

quiz.q: Predict the result: a centre is assigned the points (0, 0), (2, 0) and (4, 6). Where does it move?
Why does the inertia plotted against k always go down as k grows?
options: Because k-means is broken for large k
Because more centres can always sit closer to the points (with k = n every point is its own centre and J = 0)
It does not; it goes up
quiz.explain: That is why you look for an elbow, where adding centres stops paying off, instead of the minimum.

quiz.q: Two runs of k-means on the same data give inertias 278 and 73. What should you do?
options: Keep the run with inertia 73: the other got stuck in a poor local minimum
Keep 278 because it is more cautious
quiz.explain: Different starts can end in different local minima. The objective tells you which is better: lower inertia means tighter clusters.

quiz.q: How do many vector databases use k-means to speed up retrieval for LLM applications?
options: They cluster the embeddings and compare a query only with points in the nearest clusters
They train the language model with k-means
They use k-means to tokenise text
They do not; k-means is unrelated
quiz.explain: An inverted-file (IVF) index assigns every stored vector to a k-means centre. At query time only the closest few clusters are searched, trading a little accuracy for a big speed-up.

problems.title: Assign and update with plain lists
problems.prompt:
Points and centres are lists of [x, y] pairs. Write

  • assign(points, centres): a list with, for each point, the index of its nearest centre (squared distance is enough, no square root needed).
  • update(points, labels, k): a list of k new centres, each the mean of the points with that label. If a cluster is empty, put its centre at [0.0, 0.0].

tests.name: empty cluster does not crash

hints: assign: labels.append(min(range(len(centres)), key=lambda j: sqdist(p, centres[j])))
update: members = [p for p, l in zip(points, labels) if l == j]
if not members: centres.append([0.0, 0.0]) else: centres.append([sum(p[0] for p in members) / len(members), sum(p[1] for p in members) / len(members)])

problems.title: k-means in NumPy
problems.prompt:
The starter makes 120 synthetic points in three blobs. Write kmeans(X, init, iters) that starts from the centres init (shape (k, 2)) and repeats the two steps iters times (or until the centres stop moving). Return (centres, labels, inertia).

Broadcasting does the assignment in one line: X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :] has shape (n, k, 2); square, sum over the last axis to get an (n, k) table of squared distances, then argmin(axis=1).

Then try a bad start, such as two centres inside the same blob, and compare inertias.

tests.name: finds the three blobs
tests.code:
C, labels, J = kmeans(X, X[[0, 40, 80]])
true = np.array([[-2, 1], [2, 1.5], [0, -2]])
for t in true:
    assert np.min(np.linalg.norm(C - t, axis=1)) < 0.3, f'expected a centre near {t}, got centres {np.round(C, 2)}'

tests.name: labels and inertia agree
tests.code:
C, labels, J = kmeans(X, X[[0, 40, 80]])
assert np.shape(labels) == (120,), f'one label per point, got shape {np.shape(labels)}'
J2 = ((X - C[labels]) ** 2).sum()
assert abs(J - J2) < 1e-6 and J > 0, f'inertia should be the total squared distance to the assigned centres ({J2:.3f}), got {J}'

tests.name: a bad start ends worse
tests.code:
_, _, good = kmeans(X, X[[0, 40, 80]])
_, _, bad = kmeans(X, np.array([X[40], X[41], [-1.0, -0.5]]))
assert bad > 1.5 * good, f'two centres in one blob and one between the other two should get stuck with higher inertia ({bad:.1f} vs {good:.1f}); compute inertia from the final centres and labels'

if np.allclose(newC, C): break, then C = newC. After the loop, recompute labels and inertia = ((X - C[labels]) ** 2).sum()
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.vstack([rng.normal(c, 0.5, size=(40, 2)) for c in ([-2, 1], [2, 1.5], [0, -2])])   # shape (120, 2)

def kmeans(X, init, iters=50):
    C = np.array(init, dtype=float)
    for _ in range(iters):
        D = ((X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=-1)
        labels = D.argmin(axis=1)
        newC = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) if np.any(labels == j) else C[j] for j in range(len(C))])
        if np.allclose(newC, C):
            break
        C = newC
    D = ((X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=-1)
    labels = D.argmin(axis=1)
    inertia = ((X - C[labels]) ** 2).sum()
    return C, labels, inertia
